bugs: Edits made in the same second as the job read the rows are lost. synced_at is set to the read time, and timestamp columns only store whole seconds, so a probe where updated_at equals synced_at left the row not ready (impl-2 has the same bug).

WithoutOverlapping('stock-push') sends every push through one global lock. At about 50 jobs per peak, with a slow API and releaseAfter(30) polling, the jobs at the back can reach retryUntil (14 min) and fail. Nothing is lost because failed() clears the claim, but this causes repeated failed/re-queued jobs and wastes throughput where a rate limiter was needed.

failed() clears sync_started_at with no check that the claim is still this job's. If a claim expired and the row was claimed again, clearing it can cause a duplicate send. retryUntil being shorter than the claim TTL makes this unlikely.

app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:38 uses the fully-qualified \DateTimeInterface inline instead of importing it
app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:79 the whereNotNull('sync_started_at') filter in failed() does nothing useful
strengths: The job only loads rows that are still claimed (claimed() scope), so a job delivered twice by SQS or run a second time sends nothing. A probe confirmed one HTTP call.
synced_at uses the time captured before the request, so edits made while the request is in flight leave the row ready
Each claim batch runs in a transaction with lockForUpdate, and the schedule uses onOneServer plus withoutOverlapping, which is safe across the three scheduler containers
Bookkeeping updates use toBase() so updated_at is not touched, with a short comment explaining why
Handles 429 by releasing with Retry-After, capped at 300s with a 5s floor; uses retryUntil, which is shorter than the claim TTL; failed() releases the claim

Thorough Pest tests: a dataset for the ready-state matrix (including the exact 15-minute boundary and an abandoned claim on an already-synced row), Retry-After cap and floor, an end-to-end failure followed by re-dispatch, and a check that updated_at is preserved

bugs: The job never checks that its rows are still claimed: handle() loads every non-disabled row by id. An SQS redelivery, or a job that runs after its claim expired and the row was claimed again, sends the same data again. A probe running the job twice made 2 HTTP calls, which breaks the 'sent exactly once per change' requirement.

There is no shared limit on how many requests hit the API at once. About 50 jobs at peak all fire at a slow API, and 429s only cause each job to back off on its own, so the API keeps getting hammered and the jobs use up their retryUntil window.
Edits made in the same second as the request are lost because timestamps only store whole seconds; a probe confirmed this (impl-1 has the same bug).
failed() clears sync_started_at for all ids without checking which job owns the claim, so it can wipe out a newer claim and cause a duplicate send.

The dispatcher identifies its claim by an exact match on a whole-second claimedAt value (where sync_started_at = claimedAt). This only stays safe because onOneServer stops two dispatchers running in the same second; it is a fragile way to mark ownership.

tests/Feature/Stock/PushStockAllocationsTest.php:47 the 'can run twice' test never checks how many requests were sent, so it hides the duplicate-send bug

strengths: Claims rows with a conditional update that re-applies readyToSync, iterating with chunkById, which works correctly while rows are being modified
partition() splits accepted and unknown SKUs cleanly; unknown rows are disabled and their claim is cleared
Fillable is limited to sku and quantity
Uses toBase() for bookkeeping writes; 429 releases with a capped Retry-After; retryUntil is shorter than the claim TTL; failed() releases the claim
Simpler and leaner than impl-1, and uses modern attributes throughout

v.rationale:
I ranked impl-1 first. Both implementations pass their own suites (33 and 26 tests) and share the same overall design: a claim column, a readyToSync scope, toBase() writes, release on 429 using Retry-After, retryUntil shorter than the 15-minute claim, and failed() releasing the claim.

The deciding difference is whether a job can send the same rows twice. Impl-1's job only processes rows that are still claimed, so a job that SQS delivers twice, or that runs again after the rows were synced, sends nothing; a probe confirmed this. Impl-2 resends whatever it is given, and a probe showed 2 HTTP calls for a job run twice, which breaks 'sent exactly once per change'. Impl-2 also has no shared limit on API traffic, so about 50 parallel jobs hit a slow, rate-limited API at once. Impl-1 at least serialises the pushes. Its global WithoutOverlapping lock is not the right tool (RateLimited or Redis::throttle would be) and can make jobs fail and get re-queued under load, but it does not lose data.

Both lose edits made in the same second as the request because timestamps only store whole seconds; probes confirmed this in both. Impl-1's tests are clearly stronger: a dataset covering the ready states and boundaries, the Retry-After floor, and an end-to-end failure followed by re-dispatch. Impl-2 is a little simpler, but its tests are thinner, and one of them ('can run twice') hides its duplicate-send bug.
